passage:
Kishore found Ujjwal in the office canteen in Hyderabad, holding a tea he wasn't drinking. 'The client cancelled,' Kishore said. 'Six months of work. I keep thinking I'm finished here.'
Ujjwal pulled out a chair for him. 'Sit. Did I ever tell you about my first company?'
Kishore shook his head.
'At twenty-one, two friends and I started a bike-repair app. Took money from my father. Shut down in eight months. I didn't answer my phone for a week.'
He said it plainly, the way you'd describe a train you missed.
'It was the worst year I've had. It also taught me I like building things with people more than I like being the boss. And that I can survive a big failure.' He shrugged. 'You'll survive this one. Tomorrow, let's list what the client actually said. Then we decide what's next.'
Kishore finally drank his tea.

qa.q: How long did Ujjwal's first company last before it shut down?
qa.a: It shut down in eight months.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he said 'I keep thinking I'm finished here'?
qa.a: He felt crushed and afraid that one cancelled project meant the end of his career at the company.

qa.q: What made Ujjwal's way of supporting Kishore effective?
qa.a: He shared his own failure plainly, showed what it had taught him, and offered a concrete next step, so Kishore felt less alone and less hopeless.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt telling Kishore about his failed first company?
qa.a: Ujjwal seemed calm about it now, describing it plainly like a missed train, and willing to share it so Kishore would feel less alone.

grounding: It shows a person who can now speak plainly of an old failure as a chapter that taught resilience and clarified values, and who uses it to support someone else.

passage:
'Don't say it's fine, Anand bhaiya. It's not fine.'
'I wasn't going to say that.'
Disha pushed the report card across the kitchen table. 'Fifty-two. Everyone in my class is going to know.'
'Probably,' Anand said, pouring two glasses of water. 'Everyone in my class knew I failed Class 12.'
She looked up. 'You failed? Properly failed?'
'Properly. Chemistry and maths. I repeated the whole year. Papa didn't talk to me for about a week.'
'You never told me that.'
'You were eight. Now you're not.' He sat down. 'That year was horrible. I also found out I'm stubborn in a good way. And I stopped caring what the colony aunties thought. Mostly.'
Disha almost smiled. 'Mostly?'
'Mostly. So. Tomorrow, show me which questions went wrong. Tonight, just eat something.'
'You're not going to lecture me?'
'I'm drinking water. That's the lecture.'

qa.q: Which subjects did Anand fail in Class 12?
How can you tell Disha is starting to feel a little better by the end?
qa.a: She almost smiles and teases back with 'Mostly?', which shows her fear is easing as her brother talks.

qa.q: What did Anand do well in talking to Disha?
qa.a: He spoke about his own failure plainly, didn't lecture or pretend it was fine, and gave her one small step for tomorrow.

qa.q: What is it like for Disha to learn her brother once failed?
qa.a: It surprises her and makes her result feel less shameful, because someone she looks up to came through the same thing.

grounding: It shows a young man speaking plainly of a past failure as a chapter that taught him resilience, and using it to support his younger sister.
